_note: Coach cards (Sep 28 2026): the one coaching idea each coach card teaches (idea + lesson, original Futbol Island writing for children, never a quote), career highlights, and sources. Careers are in playerCareers.json (role "coach"), blurbs and strengths in playerProfiles.json. Current coaches were checked to be in their job in September 2026.

Luis Enrique.lesson: When the ball is lost, the nearest players jump in together within seconds. One presser gets dribbled past; three together win the ball back.

Mikel Arteta.lesson: Corners and free kicks are practised like planned moves: every player has a job, such as blocking a path or running to the near post, so a dead ball becomes a chance.
highlights: Premier League Manager of the Season 2025–26

sources.title: Arteta wins Manager of the Season (Arsenal.com)

Hansi Flick.lesson: The defenders step up together toward halfway. That squeezes the space, and a striker who runs too early is caught offside. It only works if the whole line moves as one.

sources.title: Hansi Flick extends contract until 2028 (FC Barcelona)

Carlo Ancelotti.lesson: Instead of forcing one system, pick the shape that lets your best players shine, then keep the whole squad calm and happy.
highlights: League titles in Italy, England, France, Germany and Spain

sources.title: Carlo Ancelotti signs Brazil extension until 2030 (FIFA)

Luis de la Fuente.lesson: He coached many of Spain’s players in the youth teams, so they already knew each other’s runs. Playing together for years builds an understanding you can’t buy.

Jürgen Klopp.lesson: The moment you lose the ball, hunt it straight back. The other team is not organised yet, so winning it there can be the best chance of the game.

sources.title: Jürgen Klopp appointed Germany head coach (Bundesliga)

Zinedine Zidane (coach).lesson: Zidane rotated his players so everyone stayed fresh and felt important. A whole squad, not just eleven players, wins a long season.

José Mourinho.lesson: Defend in a tight block so there is no space behind, then break forward quickly when you win the ball, before the other team can get back.

Diego Simeone.lesson: Two lines of four stay close together and slide as one toward the ball. The gaps are so small that the other team has to pass around the outside.

Vincent Kompany (coach).lesson: The goalkeeper and centre-backs pass short to draw the opponents forward. When they press, space opens behind them, and one sharp pass starts the attack.
highlights: Premier League winner as a City player

Thomas Tuchel.lesson: Tuchel often switches between a back four and a back three. One extra centre-back lets the wing-backs push high, so the team defends safely and still attacks wide.

sources.title: England v Spain, Tuchel reaction (England Football, Sep 2026)

Lionel Scaloni.idea: A team that works for its star
Lionel Scaloni.lesson: Scaloni built a hard-working midfield that won the ball and covered space, so Messi could save his energy for the moments that decide games.

sources.title: Scaloni on his Argentina future (Mundo Albiceleste, Sep 2026)

Xabi Alonso.lesson: Leverkusen played three centre-backs, with wing-backs who stayed wide and high. That stretched the defence and left gaps between the lines for the playmakers.

sources.title: Xabi Alonso appointed Chelsea manager (Chelsea FC)

Enzo Maresca.lesson: When his team has the ball, a full-back steps into midfield beside the holding midfielder. That extra player in the middle helps keep the ball and stops counter-attacks.

sources.title: Maresca appointed Man City manager (Al Jazeera)

Unai Emery.lesson: Emery watches hours of video of every opponent, then gives each player a small, clear job for that game. Knowing their habits helps you beat them.

sources.title: Emery on rotation v Coventry (VAVEL, Sep 2026)

Andoni Iraola.lesson: Each player picks up an opponent near the ball and presses hard and fast. If everyone commits, the other team has no easy pass and has to kick it long.
highlights: Promotion to La Liga with Rayo Vallecano

Cristian Chivu.lesson: Three centre-backs protect the goal while two wing-backs run the whole touchline: defenders when the other team attacks, wingers when Inter attack.
highlights: Treble winner as an Inter player (2010)

sources.title: Serie A 2026/27 head coaches (Lega Serie A)

Luciano Spalletti.lesson: At Roma he played Totti as a “false nine”: the striker drops into midfield, the defenders don’t know whether to follow, and runners burst into the space he leaves.

sources.title: Serie A 2026/27 head coaches (Lega Serie A)

Massimiliano Allegri.lesson: A match has moments: sometimes you attack, sometimes you sit tight and protect a lead. Allegri’s teams knew when to be patient, and that wins titles.

sources.title: Serie A 2026/27 head coaches (Lega Serie A)

Rúben Amorim.lesson: Three centre-backs, two wing-backs and two inside forwards: in attack the wing-backs push up, so five players stretch the defence across the whole width.
highlights: Portuguese League Cups with Braga and Sporting

sources.title: AC Milan appoints Rúben Amorim (AC Milan)

Michael Carrick.lesson: Carrick played with his head up. Before the ball arrives, look over both shoulders, then pass to the side of the pitch with more space.
highlights: Champions League winner as a player (2008)

Sarina Wiegman.lesson: Wiegman gives every player a clear job and keeps a settled team, so players know where their teammates will be. A calm plan beats panic in a final.

sources.title: Five years of Sarina Wiegman (England Football, Sep 2026)

Emma Hayes.idea: Fit the plan to the players
Emma Hayes.lesson: Hayes studies what each player does best and shapes the plan around it, then changes the shape during a game if it isn’t working.
highlights: First Ballon d’Or Women’s Coach of the Year (2024)

Pere Romeu.lesson: Barça spread out in set positions so there is always a free teammate. Pass to make a 2 v 1, then play the ball to whoever is free.

Jonatan Giráldez.lesson: Giráldez’s teams press high as a unit: lose the ball near the other goal, win it back there, and you are already close to scoring.

Rinus Michels.lesson: Players swap positions during play: a defender can attack and a forward can defend. When one player moves up, a teammate fills the gap, so the shape never breaks.

Alex Ferguson.lesson: His teams kept attacking right to the end, and many games were won in the last minutes, like the 1999 Champions League final comeback.

Arrigo Sacchi.lesson: The whole team stays about 25 metres from front to back and guards space, not players. Close together, they can press the ball as a pack.

Johan Cruyff (coach).lesson: In a rondo, players in a circle keep the ball away from one or two in the middle. It trains quick touches, scanning and triangles, the heart of Barça’s style.
highlights: 4 La Liga titles in a row (1991–1994)

Pep Guardiola.lesson: Players spread into five lanes across the pitch so there is always a free passing option. Move the ball quickly to find a teammate between the opponent’s lines.

Bob Paisley.lesson: Paisley’s Liverpool passed the ball, then moved into space for the return. Short passes and constant movement are simple to learn and hard to stop.

Ernst Happel.lesson: Happel’s defenders stepped forward together to catch strikers offside, and his teams pressed high to win the ball near the other goal.

Helenio Herrera.lesson: A spare defender, the libero (“free man”), stays behind the others to sweep up any ball that gets through. Then the team hits fast counter-attacks.

Vicente del Bosque.lesson: Spain passed and passed. If you keep the ball, the other team can’t score, and they get tired chasing it.

Marcello Lippi.lesson: Lippi’s 2006 Italy had ten different goalscorers at the World Cup. When every player can score and defend, opponents can’t just stop one star.

Giovanni Trapattoni.lesson: Some defenders mark a player man-to-man while others guard zones of the pitch. Mixing both keeps a team solid and ready to break forward.
highlights: League titles in Italy, Germany, Portugal and Austria

Bill Shankly.lesson: Shankly’s training used small-sided games and passing against wooden boards, so players got many touches and learned to control and pass quickly.

Matt Busby.lesson: Busby picked teenagers from the youth team for the first team. Young players who learn the club’s way together can grow into champions.

Brian Clough.lesson: Clough wanted football played on the ground: keep the ball low and pass to feet, because a high ball is harder to control.

Arsène Wenger.lesson: Wenger changed what his players ate and how they stretched and rested. A body looked after well trains harder and plays faster.

Valeriy Lobanovskyi.lesson: Lobanovskyi measured runs, passes and tackles to plan training. Every player had clear tasks, and the team pressed together to make the pitch small.

Béla Guttmann.lesson: Four forwards and two midfielders: Guttmann’s Benfica attacked with lots of players and aimed to score one goal more than the other team.

Vittorio Pozzo.lesson: Pozzo’s “metodo” shape used a centre-half who dropped back to help defend and then started attacks: an early version of today’s holding midfielder.

Mário Zagallo.lesson: As a player Zagallo was a winger who ran back to help midfield. As a coach he used that idea, so Brazil could defend with more players and still attack.

Telê Santana.lesson: Telê wanted beautiful attacking football: short passes, dribbles and lots of players joining the attack, with the players enjoying their game.

Jupp Heynckes.lesson: Heynckes’s 2013 Bayern defended as hard as they attacked: even the star wingers ran back. Balance between attack and defence wins trebles.

Alf Ramsey.lesson: Ramsey left out traditional wingers and used hard-working midfielders who could defend and attack. Four in midfield made England hard to beat.

Pia Sundhage.lesson: Sundhage asked her teams to keep the ball and play with courage, and built a happy team where players felt free to try things.

Jill Ellis.lesson: Ellis used her whole squad at tournaments, so fresh legs were always ready. A team with 23 ready players beats a team that depends on 11.
highlights: FIFA Women’s Coach of the Year 2015 and 2019

Silvia Neid.lesson: Germany won the 2007 World Cup without letting in a single goal. Neid’s teams stayed compact, won their duels and made every opponent work hard.
